title: Permission catalog UX hypothesis and wires
content:
Context and purpose:
This doc collects a compact UX hypothesis and wireframe notes for a unified Permission Catalog experience: a single place in Console to discover roles, create scoped API keys and service accounts, preview effective permissions, and run compact audit inspections. The goal is to reduce support load (help users find why a token failed), make it straightforward to create least-privilege credentials, and provide compact audit views that are readable in SRE/SEC triage workflows.

Why we need a Permission Catalog (short):
- Current Console RBAC views are fragmented: role templates live in one panel, service accounts in another, API key rotation flows in a modal.
- Support and customers repeatedly ask for a way to see "what does this role actually allow" and to create tokens scoped to a single model/route without a ton of clicks.
- Audit team wants quick pivot: from an API key to the user/service account to recent actions that used that key.

Primary goals and success metrics (experiment):
- Reduce number of clicks to create a scoped API key from 8 -> <=4 for common patterns (create key for embeddings-only usage).
- Decrease support tickets asking "why did this call 403" by surfacing a live policy preview and last-used timestamp on tokens.
- 25% adoption of Permission Catalog by teams creating new keys in first 90 days.

Personas:
- Platform engineer (SRE): wants compact audit view and quick ability to revoke/bounce keys used by a failing job.
- App developer: wants to get a key scoped to a single model and route with minimal friction.
- Security reviewer: wants to browse role templates, compare two roles, and run a policy simulator for sample requests.

High-level product ideas summarized (why each matters):
- Permission Catalog landing: searchable list of role templates, service accounts, and active API tokens with filters (by team, tag, last-used).
  - Why: single discoverability surface.
- Live policy preview / simulator: enter a sample request (model + route + resource) and see allow/deny and which policy rule matched.
  - Why: reduces "mystery 403" tickets and supports on-boarding.
- Scoped Key creation flow: inline role pick + quick presets (embeddings-only, generate-read-only, admin-lite) with an accordion for advanced constraints (IP, TTL, allowed-models, allowed-routes).
  - Why: lowers barrier to least-privilege.
- Service account lifecycle panel: create, grant team roles, rotate keys, attach description and owner. Show lineage: which keys were issued from the service account, which were used.
  - Why: improves traceability and rotation hygiene.
- Compact Audit Inspector: a condensed chronological view that pivots from token -> service account -> user -> last 50 events (filters: route, status, start-end). Include a compressed event summary (human readable).
  - Why: faster triage flows for SRE and CS.

Wireframe notes (screen-by-screen):
1) Landing: Permission Catalog
- Top: global search + quick-create button (Key | Service account | Role template).
- Left: filters: team, kind (role/service-account/api-key), last-used bucket, tag.
- Main: two-column list: left column = Role/templates cards (compact), right column = Active tokens list.
- Card highlights: role name, description, sample routes allowed (comma-separated), last edited, "Preview" button that opens policy simulator.
- For tokens show obfuscated key id, owner (service account/user), last-used (ago), TTL, and small action menu (revoke, copy, rotate).

2) Role detail editor (inline modal)
- Top: role name + short description + version selector.
- Middle: permission pivot with two tabs: "Compact rules" (human readable bullet list) and "Raw policy" (collapsible JSON).
- Live simulator bar at bottom of modal: mini-form (route, model, resource id) + result chip (ALLOW / DENY) + matched-rule link.
- Inline "create child role" button: clone + restrict.

3) Scoped Key creation flow (3-step in single page):
- Step 1: pick principal (user / service account) + attach to team (auto-suggest).
- Step 2: pick template preset (Embeddings-only, Chat-limited, Full-generate) OR custom role pick. Quick toggles for allowed-models and allowed-routes.
- Step 3: constraints: TTL (1h/24h/7d/custom), CIDR allowlist, max requests/day. Final preview shows effective permissions and sample cURL. Provide a one-click copy of the token after creation (token shown once).

4) Service Account lifecycle screen
- Top: summary card with SA name, owner, linked teams. Buttons: Create key, Rotate, Deactivate.
- Middle: Key timeline: rows for each key with created_at, last_used, used_by_jobs (badge), and rotation policy. Action: rotate, revoke.
- Right: "where used" panel: shows last 20 calls using this SA (route, outcome, truncated request id).

5) Compact Audit Inspector (compact modal used across console)
- Trigger: from token card, from job run in Jobs list, or from support ticket link.
- Body: top-line summary: "Token ABC... used by service-account X — last call 12m ago". Below: collapsible last 50 events rendered as human phrases (e.g., "2025-01-07 12:13 UTC — generate.response — model: redwood/gpt-3x — 200 OK — tokens: 128").
- Quick actions inline: Revoke token, rotate, copy forensic download link (CSV), open full audit log in Security console.

Microcopy suggestions (short, non-blocking):
- Create scoped key CTA: "Create token (recommended: embeddings-only)"
- Live preview result: "This request will be allowed because it matches rule: embeddings-readonly-v1"
- Warning on long-lived keys: "Long TTL increases blast radius. Consider 24h tokens for dev/test."

Accessibility and edge UX notes:
- Ensure role names and summaries have aria-describedby linking to full policy.
- Keyboard flows for modal simulator: tab order ends on Run -> Result -> Close.
- When copying a key, show ephemeral toast with time-limited copy hint: "Copied — token shown once".

Backlog & grooming (initial prioritized stories):
- PCAT-01: Permission Catalog landing — search + filters (priority P0).
- PCAT-02: Scoped Key creation flow (presets + TTL + IP allowlist) (P0).
- PCAT-03: Live policy simulator (embedded) (P1).
- PCAT-04: Service Account timeline + where-used panel (P1).
- PCAT-05: Compact Audit Inspector (modal) + CSV export (P1).
- PCAT-06: Role templatization & versioning UX (P2).
- PCAT-07: Metrics eventing for key creation and revocation (instrumentation) (P2).

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Do we allow creating keys with multiple role attachments or restrict to single effective role? (security: single role preferred; dev ergonomics: multiple roles sometimes needed).
- TTL default: should dev orgs get 7d by default? (proposal: default 24h for orgs < 50 seats, 7d for >50 with audit-enabled).
- Where to store policy simulator sample requests? ephemeral per-user or saved to team prompt-sets? (keep ephemeral for now).
- Should the compact audit inspector be in product (Console) or link to Security console for enterprise customers? (tech constraint: cross-service auth surface; proposal: include compact view for all, full logs link for Enterprise).

Next steps and short runway (owner: Maya):
- 2/Week: Sketch high-fidelity wireframes for Landing + Scoped Key flow (deliverable: figma file with annotated interactions).
- Product sync: schedule with SRE and Sec next week to confirm last-used telemetry availability (owners: Ethan & Nikhil).
- Engineering spike: feasibility of inline simulator (policy evaluation API and cost) — 1 sprint, EPIC: PCAT-sim-spike.
- Put PCAT-01/02 into next sprint planning, attach acceptance criteria and instrumentation tickets.

Notes and references (working links):
- Jira: JIRA-1234 (Permission Catalog EPIC), JIRA-1407 (Policy simulator spike)
- Design: figma.com/redwood/permission-catalog/sketches (working draft)
- Slack: #console-permissions — conversation Ts2k9f contains customer quote: "We just want to issue a key for embeddings, not full generate"

Unresolved UX trade-offs (for retrospective):
- Inline vs separate page for scoped-key creation (inline reduces context switching but increases surface complexity).
- Showing raw policy JSON by default or hiding it under "advanced" (we propose hide by default).

Appendix: short example of humanized policy translation for wireframe"
- Raw rule: { allow: true, routes: ["/v1/embeddings"], models: ["redwood/emb-1"], ttl: "24h" }
- Compact translation: "Allows embedding calls to model redwood/emb-1 for 24 hours."

-- end of doc --
